boilerplate.section_intro: This section consists of questions and problems involving quantitative reasoning.  Each question is followed by four possible responses.  Choose the correct answer and mark its number in the appropriate place on the answer sheet.

boilerplate.general_comments_title: General Comments about the Quantitative Reasoning Section
general_comments: The figures accompanying some of the problems are provided to help solve the problems, but are not necessarily drawn to scale.  Therefore, do not rely on the figures alone to deduce line length, angle size, and so forth.
If a line in a figure appears to be straight, you may assume that it is in fact a straight line.
When a geometric term (side, radius, area, volume, etc.) appears in a problem, it refers to a term whose value is greater than 0, unless stated otherwise.
When \(\sqrt{a}\) (a > 0) appears in a problem, it refers to the positive root of a.
"0" is neither a positive nor a negative number.

clusters.intro:
Study the table below, then answer the four questions that follow.

The table presents data on 5 models of small motorboats that are used on the Tonga Islands.  The models are marked with the letters A-E.
Next to each model several data are indicated: the engine volume of the boat (in cc); the number of kilometres that it travels when it needs one litre of fuel; the type of fuel that the boat needs; the price of a new boat (in pananga, the local currency on the Tonga Islands); and the annual drop in value (in pananga).
The fuel prices on the Tonga Islands appear in a separate small table.

For example: A new boat of model B costs 6,000 pananga, and after a year its value will be 5,700 pananga.  When such a boat sails a distance of 25 km it needs one litre of petrol, and when it sails a distance of 50 km it needs 2 litres, and so on.

Study the graphs below, then answer the four questions that follow. The graphs present data on the water consumption of two families, A and B, over the course of a certain year. The upper graph indicates the quantity of water (in m³) that each of the two families needed in each of the months of the year (see key). The lines connecting the points in the graph are auxiliary lines only. The lower graphs present the distribution of the water consumption of each of the families according to five uses: cooking, laundry, washing, cleaning the house and flushing the toilets. The distribution of the water consumption of each of the families is fixed throughout all the months of the year. For example: In September family B needed 400 m³ of water altogether. 15% of this quantity was used for laundry.

questions.stem:
Given:  2x + 2y = 340

3x + 3y = ?

methods.text: \(2x+2y = 340\) means \(x+y = 170\), so \(3x+3y = 3 \times 170 = 510\). The target is a multiple of the given, so no solving is needed.
Neither \(x\) nor \(y\) can be found — one equation, two unknowns. The question asks only for the combination that is determined.

questions.stem:
In a certain hotel there are F floors, and on each floor there are x large rooms and y small rooms.

Which of the following expressions expresses the difference between the number of large rooms and the number of small rooms in the entire hotel?

methods.text: Each floor holds \(x-y\) more large rooms than small, and there are \(F\) floors, so the difference across the hotel is \(F(x-y)\).
Take \(F=2, x=5, y=3\): 10 large rooms against 6 small, a difference of 4. Only \(F(x-y) = 2 \times 2\) gives 4.

questions.stem:
In the accompanying figure is triangle ABC.

Given:  AD = DC = DB
     ∡BCA = 40°

∡BAC = ?

Given:  \(a! = 24 \cdot 30\)

a = ?

methods.text: \(24\cdot30=720\), and 720 is a factorial you should know by sight: \(6!\). The small factorials — \(1,2,6,24,120,720,5040\) — are worth memorising, because questions hide them inside ordinary-looking products.
You can also read it without multiplying. \(24=4!\), and \(30=5\cdot6\), so \(24\cdot30=4!\cdot5\cdot6=6!\) by definition. Building up from a smaller factorial beats computing.

questions.stem: Gilad solved 200 arithmetic exercises in \(3\frac{2}{3}\) hours. How many arithmetic exercises will Gilad solve in one hour and fifty minutes if he works at a speed that is 2 times slower than his usual speed?

methods.text: His usual rate is \(200 \div \frac{11}{3} = \frac{600}{11}\) an hour; half that is \(\frac{300}{11}\). In \(\frac{11}{6}\) hours that is 50.
“Two times slower” halves the rate and doubles the time. The awkward fractions cancel exactly, which is the sign the numbers were chosen deliberately.

questions.stem: A sports club has 300 members: 200 adults and 100 children. 120 members of the club are registered for a soccer class. 60 members of the club are registered for a swimming class. How many of the members of the club, at most, are adults who are not registered for a soccer class and not for a swimming class?
How many numbers between 1 and 100 are divisible by both 4 and 6 without a remainder?

methods.text: Divisible by both 4 and 6 means divisible by their lowest common multiple, which is 12 — not by their product, 24. That distinction is the whole question.
Multiples of 12 up to 100 run \(12, 24, \ldots, 96\), which is \(\lfloor 100/12 \rfloor = 8\) of them.

questions.stem: \(0 < a\) , \(0 < \dfrac{a + b}{a} < 1\) Which of the following inequalities is necessarily true?

methods.text: \(a\) is positive, so multiplying through by it does not flip anything: \(0<a+b<a\). Subtracting \(a\) from all three parts leaves \(-a<b<0\).
A fraction strictly between 0 and 1 means the numerator is positive and smaller than the denominator. Positive gives \(b>-a\); smaller than \(a\) gives \(b<0\).
\(a=2,\ b=-1\) satisfies the given, since \(\frac12\) lies between 0 and 1. It has \(b\) negative and \(|b|<a\), which is exactly option (1) and kills the other three.

questions.stem:
In the accompanying figure ABCD is the square that is inscribed in a circle whose radius is 1 cm.

Given:  AE = ED

What is the area of triangle AED (in cm²)?

The letters A, B, C, D and E represent digits between 1 and 9.

Which of the following expressions is equal to the decimal fraction AB.CDE ?

methods.text: Read the number by place value: \(A\) is in the tens place, \(B\) the units, then \(C\), \(D\), \(E\) in the tenths, hundredths and thousandths. That is \(10A + B + \frac{C}{10} + \frac{D}{100} + \frac{E}{1000}\).
Take \(A{=}1, B{=}2, C{=}3, D{=}4, E{=}5\), so the number is \(12.345\). Only option (4) evaluates to \(12.345\).

In a class there are 8 girls and x boys.  \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the number of boys is equal to \(\frac{1}{4}\) of all the students in the class.

x = ?

methods.text: \(\frac x3 = \frac{8+x}{4}\). Cross-multiplying gives \(4x = 24+3x\), so \(x = 24\).
With \(x=24\) there are 32 students: a third of the boys is 8, and a quarter of 32 is 8. The other options fail this in one line each.

The number x was multiplied by itself, and afterwards the result was multiplied by 4.
If 64 is subtracted from the number that was obtained, we will get the number 0.

Which of the following statements is correct?
options: x can only be the number 0
x can only be the number 4
x can be two numbers only, among them the number 0
x can be two numbers only, among them the number –4

methods.text: The description is \(4x^2 - 64 = 0\), so \(x^2 = 16\) and \(x = \pm4\). Two values, one of which is \(-4\).

Translating the words is the whole task: “multiplied by itself” is the square, and it happens before the multiplication by 4. Option (3) is there for anyone who solves \(4x^2 - 64x = 0\) instead and picks up a root of 0.

methods.text: Nested percentages multiply. \(a\) cancels entirely, which is why the answer is a bare number.

questions.stem:
Given:  \(x = 2 \cdot \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^{7}\) ,   \(0 < x\)

x = ?

methods.text: Clear the bracket: \(x = \dfrac{2x^7}{2^7} = \dfrac{x^7}{2^6}\), so \(x^7 = 64x\) and, dividing by \(x\) since \(x>0\), \(x^6 = 64\). Hence \(x = 2\).
Four options and one substitution each: \(x=2\) gives \(2 \cdot 1^7 = 2\) immediately. Faster than solving when the options are plain numbers.

questions.stem:
The water level of a certain lake is now 1 metre lower than the height of the dam that is at the end of the lake.  When the water reaches the height of the dam it overflows from the dam.
Each day the water level of the lake rises by 3 cm.
The day that is beginning now and ending 24 hours from now is called "day 1".

The water will begin to overflow from the dam during day –

methods.text: The gap is 100 cm closing at 3 cm a day, so \(\frac{100}{3} = 33\frac13\) days. The level passes the dam during the 34th day.
A fractional answer to a “which day” question always rounds up — the event happens inside the next whole day, not at the end of the previous one.

\(|x| = 13\) ,  \(|y| = 4\)

How many different values can the expression \(|x - y|\) have?

methods.text: Flipping the signs of both \(x\) and \(y\) negates \(x-y\) and leaves \(|x-y|\) untouched, so the four sign combinations collapse into two mirror pairs. Fix \(x=13\) and only two cases remain.
With \(x=13\): \(|13-4|=9\) and \(|13+4|=17\). Two distinct values.

methods.text: \(ab-b^2 = b(a-b)\), so over the common denominator \(b(a-b)\) the expression is \(\dfrac{a^2+b^2-2ab}{b(a-b)} = \dfrac{(a-b)^2}{b(a-b)} = \dfrac{a-b}{b}\).
Take \(a=3, b=1\): the expression is \(\frac{10}{2} - 3 = 2\), and \(\frac{a-b}{b} = 2\).
The numerator turning into \((a-b)^2\) is the square identity read backwards — the same move that decides most questions in this subcategory.

questions.stem: A basketball player is shooting at a basket. If she scores a basket on a certain shot, the probability that she will score a basket on the next shot is \(\frac{1}{2}\). If she does not score a basket on a certain shot, the probability that she will score a basket on the next shot is \(\frac{1}{4}\). It is known that the player scored a basket on the first shot. What is the probability that she will score a basket on the third shot?

A tortoise and a hare competed in a race that was 100 metres long. The tortoise began to run at the beginning of the race, and advanced at a constant speed of 0.5 metres per second. The hare began to run T seconds after the beginning of the race, and advanced at a speed that was 20 times greater than the tortoise's speed. The two of them reached the finish line together. T = ?

methods.text: Tortoise: \(\frac{100}{0.5} = 200\) seconds for the whole race. Hare: 20 times the speed is 10 m/s, so \(\frac{100}{10} = 10\) seconds.

They finish together, so the hare's late start is the difference in the two running times: \(200 - 10 = 190\). Computing each animal's own time separately, then subtracting, avoids any relative-speed setup.

questions.stem:
Given:  a < 1 , b < 1
     \(a \cdot b = M\)

Which of the following statements is correct with regard to the number M ?
options: It is necessarily positive and less than 1
It can be any number except 1
It can be any number, including 1

methods.text: \(a=b=-1\) satisfies both givens and gives \(M=1\). That single pair kills options (1), (2) and (3), since all three deny that \(M\) can be 1.

“Less than 1” leaves the whole negative half-line open, so both factors can be large negatives and the product can be made as large as you like — or as negative, by taking one factor negative and the other a small positive. Nothing is out of reach.
